Now I'm going to hop into the "Not quite as far back as way back, but still not as new as right now" machine (pat. pending ad I'm still workshopping the name). Let's look at what you already do that must probably work, or you wouldn't do it:

  1. After the movie has gone through the theatres, you release a DVD and throngs of drooling fans run to the stores and yell "Shut up and take my money!" with their fancy new copy of the movie in one hand and a few crumpled up bills in the fist made by the other hand.

  2. Some time after the Blu Ray / DVD fleecing, some of the fans grow some of their wool back and you release a new "Special Edition" version with two deleted scenes, a blooper roll including that time Natalie Portman farted and the director's commentary (that nobody will ever listen to), and some more sheep come waddling in with their fistfuls of money and buy them up.

  3. Next, you guys probably sit around and complain that the pirating has lowered the DVD sales and, as a result, you can't afford the genuine panda skin seat cover option on your new Maserati. Go hire me some lawyers to sue the poor people who stole from us.

Before the movie comes out, release the abridged version. Cut out some entertaining, but relatively unessential scenes to reduce the length of the movie by 20 minutes to half an hour. Bam, there it is. You're welcome. Good-bye.

What. What else do you want?

Why are you still reading? Oh, you want me to explain why this is a multi-million dollar stroke of pure genius and how it works? Okay, get comfy; here we go:

The movie you distribute online won't be the fully polished article. There'll still be some post processing that needs to be done, maybe some voice rework, but the quality will still be better than some shitty cam with Czechoslovakian or Korean subtitles hard encoded on it. This, coupled with the missing entertaining but not entirely essential scenes, will make people want to go see the theatrical release.

If the movie is a bomb you can make the decision on what to do with it before it's even finished production. It'd also give Ben Stiller enough time to warn his mom that his new movie won't be getting released after all. (Just kidding, she died last May)

If the movie is good...oh boy! Congratulations, you just won yourself a free viral internet advertising campaign! There'll be a whole lot of:

"Hey Bob, did you see that new [insert formulaic, blockbuster movie theme here] online?"

  • "Sure did, Deepak. Can't wait to see the finished thing in the theatre, is your wife still fat?"

"She sure is, Bob; and I'm pretty stoked to see it too. It's opening next week, wanna go see it opening night?"

  • "You bet, I can bring my fat wife and mediocre child!"

"Hooray!"

i) They already do that very effectively. They got this thing now called "The Google". You can type in a question and the answer will just pop up there.

ii) You have already advertised it in a trailer for this movie that was in another pre-release movie that had already hit the internet. I'm going to let take a moment and think about that. No, you don't. Remember all those pesky torrent sites we were talking about before? You don't have to co-ordinate with them (put the phone down, nobody's going to be able to get the Pirate Bay guys on the line for you).
